title: Increasing, Decreasing, and the First Derivative Test
subject: AP Calculus AB
objectives: Use the sign of f'(x) to determine the intervals on which a function is increasing or decreasing.
Find all critical points, including where f'(x) = 0 and where f'(x) is undefined.
Build a sign chart for f' and apply the First Derivative Test to classify local maxima and minima.
Justify increasing/decreasing and extremum conclusions with correct reasoning language.

sections.heading: The Derivative Is the Function's Direction
sections.content:
If you know the sign of a function's derivative, you know which way the function is heading. A derivative is a slope, and a slope tells you whether the graph is climbing or falling as you move left to right. This single idea — read the sign of f', conclude the direction of f — is the engine of the entire analytical-applications unit.

Concretely: where f'(x) > 0, the tangent lines slope upward, so f is *increasing* — the outputs get larger as x grows. Where f'(x) < 0, the tangent lines slope downward, so f is *decreasing*. Where f'(x) = 0, the tangent is momentarily horizontal — the function pauses, and that pause is often (but not always) the top of a hill or the bottom of a valley.

Think of hiking a trail whose elevation is f(x). Your derivative f'(x) is the steepness underfoot: positive when you're climbing, negative when you're descending, zero at a crest or a dip. To map out the whole hike — every climb, every descent, every peak and valley — you don't need to measure the elevation at thousands of points. You just need to know *where the steepness changes sign*. Those sign changes are where the interesting features live, and finding them is what this lesson is about.

sections.heading: Critical Points and the Increasing/Decreasing Test
sections.content:
The places where f could switch between increasing and decreasing are its *critical points*: interior values of x where f'(x) = 0 or where f'(x) does not exist (while f itself is still defined). These are the only candidates for a local maximum or minimum, because a function can only turn around where its slope is zero or where it has a corner/cusp.

The Increasing/Decreasing Test formalizes the direction idea: on any interval where f'(x) > 0, f is increasing; on any interval where f'(x) < 0, f is decreasing. To apply it, you find the critical points (which split the number line into intervals), then test the sign of f' on each interval. Because f' can only change sign at a critical point (for a continuous f'), one test value per interval tells you the sign on the entire interval.

A subtle but important point: f'(x) = 0 does NOT guarantee a maximum or minimum. The function f(x) = x³ has f'(0) = 0, yet x = 0 is neither — the function increases on both sides. What actually creates a local extremum is a *sign change* in f', not merely a zero. That's why the sign chart, not the list of zeros, is the real tool.

sections.heading: Building a Sign Chart for f'

steps.title: Differentiate and find critical points
steps.content: Compute f'(x). Solve f'(x) = 0 and separately find where f'(x) is undefined (but f is defined). These critical x-values are the only places the sign can change.

steps.title: Mark the critical points on a number line
steps.content: Place the critical points in order; they divide the domain into open intervals.

steps.title: Test the sign of f' in each interval
steps.content: Pick any convenient value in each interval and determine whether f'(x) is positive or negative there — you need only the sign, not the exact value.

steps.title: Translate signs into behavior
steps.content: Positive means increasing, negative means decreasing. A change from + to − is a local max; from − to + is a local min; no change means neither.

sections.heading: Intervals of Increase and Decrease
sections.content:
Find where f(x) = x⁴ − 8x² is increasing and decreasing.

Differentiate: f'(x) = 4x³ − 16x = 4x(x² − 4) = 4x(x − 2)(x + 2).

Critical points (f' = 0): x = −2, 0, 2. (f' is a polynomial, defined everywhere, so there are no 'undefined' critical points.)

Sign chart, testing each interval:
  x < −2 (try x = −3): 4(−3)(−5)(−1) = −60 < 0 → decreasing
  −2 < x < 0 (try x = −1): 4(−1)(−3)(1) = 12 > 0 → increasing
  0 < x < 2 (try x = 1): 4(1)(−1)(3) = −12 < 0 → decreasing
  x > 2 (try x = 3): 4(3)(1)(5) = 60 > 0 → increasing

So f is decreasing on (−∞, −2), increasing on (−2, 0), decreasing on (0, 2), and increasing on (2, ∞). The W-shape this describes is exactly the graph of x⁴ − 8x².

sections.heading: Don't Forget Where f' Is Undefined
sections.content: Critical points include x-values where f'(x) does not exist, not only where f'(x) = 0. For f(x) = x^(2/3), the derivative f'(x) = (2/3)x^(−1/3) is undefined at x = 0, yet f(0) = 0 is defined and is actually the function's minimum (a sharp cusp). If you only solve f'(x) = 0 you'd miss it entirely. Always ask both questions: where is f'(x) zero, and where is f'(x) undefined while f is still defined? Both kinds of points must go on your sign chart.

sections.question: If f'(x) = (x − 1)(x + 3), on which interval is f decreasing?
sections.explanation: f' = (x − 1)(x + 3) is zero at x = −3 and x = 1. Testing a point in (−3, 1), say x = 0: (−1)(3) = −3 < 0, so f is decreasing there. Outside that interval both factors share a sign, making f' positive, so f increases on (−∞, −3) and (1, ∞).

sections.heading: The First Derivative Test for Local Extrema
sections.content:
Once your sign chart is built, classifying each critical point is immediate. The First Derivative Test reads the *sign change* of f' across a critical point c:

• If f' changes from positive to negative at c, then f is increasing then decreasing — c is a local MAXIMUM.
• If f' changes from negative to positive at c, then f is decreasing then increasing — c is a local MINIMUM.
• If f' does NOT change sign at c, then c is neither a max nor a min (the function keeps going the same direction, as with x³ at 0).

The reasoning is just the picture of a hill and a valley: a peak is exactly where you stop climbing and start descending (slope goes + to −), and a valley is where you stop descending and start climbing (slope goes − to +). The test simply converts that picture into a rule about the sign of f'.

This test works even at critical points where f' is undefined (like the cusp of x^(2/3)), as long as f is continuous there — you still just check whether the sign of f' flips across the point. That generality is one reason the First Derivative Test is so reliable: it never requires the second derivative, and it handles corners and cusps that the second derivative test cannot.

sections.heading: Classifying the Extrema
sections.content:
Classify the local extrema of f(x) = x⁴ − 8x² using the sign chart from before.

Recall the signs of f'(x) = 4x(x − 2)(x + 2):
  decreasing on (−∞, −2), increasing on (−2, 0), decreasing on (0, 2), increasing on (2, ∞).

Now read the sign changes at each critical point:
  At x = −2: f' goes from − to + → local MINIMUM. Value: f(−2) = 16 − 32 = −16.
  At x = 0: f' goes from + to − → local MAXIMUM. Value: f(0) = 0.
  At x = 2: f' goes from − to + → local MINIMUM. Value: f(2) = 16 − 32 = −16.

So f has local minima at (−2, −16) and (2, −16) and a local maximum at (0, 0). The two minima share the same value because f is an even function, symmetric about the y-axis — a useful check that the work is consistent.

sections.question: A continuous function has f'(x) > 0 for x < 4 and f'(x) < 0 for x > 4. What occurs at x = 4?
options: Neither a max nor a min
sections.explanation: f' changes from positive (increasing) to negative (decreasing) at x = 4, so by the First Derivative Test the function rises then falls — a local maximum. A change from negative to positive would instead give a local minimum; inflection points are about concavity (f''), not f'.

sections.heading: Say It the Way the Rubric Wants
sections.content: On AP free response, conclusions must be justified by explicit reference to the sign of f'. Write, for example, 'f has a local maximum at x = 4 because f' changes from positive to negative there.' Stating only 'f'(4) = 0' or 'the graph goes up then down' without citing the sign change typically does not earn the justification point. Also distinguish local from absolute: the First Derivative Test finds LOCAL extrema; for absolute extrema on a closed interval you still compare with endpoint values using the Candidates Test.

sections.heading: Why the Sign of f' Controls Monotonicity
sections.content:
Why is it true that f'(x) > 0 on an interval forces f to increase there? It feels obvious, but the rigorous reason is the Mean Value Theorem from the previous lesson — and seeing the connection deepens both ideas.

Take any two points a < b in an interval where f'(x) > 0 everywhere. The MVT guarantees some c between them with f(b) − f(a) = f'(c)(b − a). Since b − a > 0 and f'(c) > 0, the product is positive, so f(b) > f(a). Because a and b were arbitrary, every later input gives a larger output: f is strictly increasing. The same argument with f'(x) < 0 gives f(b) < f(a), so f decreases. The Increasing/Decreasing Test is therefore not an assumption — it is a theorem, proved by the MVT.

This also explains why a zero of f' need not be an extremum. f'(0) = 0 for f(x) = x³, but f'(x) = 3x² is positive on both sides of 0, so by the test f increases through 0 without turning around — there's a horizontal tangent but no peak or valley. The extremum requires the slope to actually *reverse*, which is precisely a sign change. The single most common error in this topic is concluding 'f'(c) = 0, therefore extremum'; the cure is to always confirm the sign change. Mastering this distinction is what lets you read a function's entire shape from the behavior of its derivative — the skill the rest of the unit builds on.

f is increasing where f'(x) > 0 and decreasing where f'(x) < 0. Critical points occur where f'(x) = 0 or is undefined (with f defined). The First Derivative Test classifies a critical point by the sign change of f': + to − is a local maximum, − to + is a local minimum, and no sign change is neither. Justify conclusions by citing the sign change, not just that f' = 0.

aiContext: AP Calculus AB Unit 5, increasing/decreasing behavior and the First Derivative Test. The dominant error is concluding an extremum from f'(c) = 0 alone; emphasize that a local extremum requires a sign CHANGE in f' (x³ at 0 is the counterexample). Stress AP justification language: a local max/min must be justified by f' changing from positive to negative (or vice versa).
